title: You have just been given a serious diagnosis
lede: A consultant has said a word you have been fearing. The room has gone slightly unreal and they are still talking, explaining stages or options, and you are absorbing almost none of it.

blocks.text: A consultant has said a word you have been fearing. The room has gone slightly unreal and they are still talking, explaining stages or options, and you are absorbing almost none of it.

items: You will retain very little of this conversation. That is normal neurology under shock, not a failure of attention, and it is why the second appointment matters more than the first.
The prognosis figures you are about to search online are population averages, often years out of date, and frequently exclude the treatment you will actually receive.
Almost no decision has to be made today. Even in fast-moving disease, days for a second opinion are usually available and are standard practice.
The urge to protect everyone by saying nothing is powerful and it isolates you exactly when support has the most value.

items.move: Ask them to write down the diagnosis, exactly
items.detail: The precise name, type, and stage. Vague terms make everything afterwards harder, including searching for real information.

items.move: Ask for the three practical questions
items.detail: "What are my options?" "What happens if we do nothing?" "What does the best case look like?"

items.move: Record the conversation or bring someone
items.detail: Ask permission and record it on your phone, or have someone else take notes. This is normal and clinicians expect it.

items.move: Ask about the second appointment and who your named contact is
items.detail: A specialist nurse or care coordinator is often the most useful person in the whole system.

items.move: Do not make treatment decisions in the room
items.detail: Say you want to think and return with questions. That is a clinically respected response.

items.move: Ask what you should do in the next week
items.detail: Practical, immediate, bounded. It converts an abyss into a task list.

items.say: "Can you stop for a moment? I have stopped taking it in. Can you write down the diagnosis and the next step?"
"If you were me, what would you want to know that I have not thought to ask?"
"I would like a second opinion before deciding. Can you help arrange it?" — this is routine and good clinicians support it.
"I have news and I want to tell you properly. It is serious, there is a plan, and I will need you for practical things more than for reassurance."

items: Searching survival statistics at 2am on the first night. It is the single most damaging thing people do in week one.
Making financial, job, or relationship decisions in the first fortnight.
Alternative treatments that require abandoning conventional care.
Telling everyone at once and then having to manage forty people's emotions.
Reading forums for prognosis. Use them for practical coping, not for numbers.
Start one notebook: dates, drug names, doses, appointments, questions. It will be worth more than any app.
Nominate one person as the information hub so you are not repeating the news thirty times.
Sort the boring admin early — sick pay, insurance, benefits, work notification, power of attorney if relevant. It removes background dread.
Ask about the psychological support attached to your service. It exists and it is underused.

limit: If you are told something serious, ask for it in writing and ask for the name of the condition, the stage, and the next decision point. Get a second opinion for anything irreversible, and take someone with you to the next appointment. If you have thoughts of ending your life, contact a crisis line or emergency services now — that is the line where this stops being something to manage alone.
